readiness.guidance: You’re physiologically recovered and ready for moderate training stimulus, but chronic sleep debt is eroding long-term adaptation potential — prioritize sleep consistency before adding intensity.

monthly_review.summary: This month shows reduced volume and slower average pace versus last month, with improved aerobic efficiency and lower HR — consistent with a deliberate recovery- or base-building emphasis, not decline.
monthly_review.highlight: Cadence increased by 32 spm month-over-month — the largest absolute shift in any metric — and aligns with improved aerobic TE and lower HR, suggesting more economical, relaxed running despite slower pace.

goal_tracker.message: To match last month’s 82.4 km would require 34.1 km across 5 remaining sessions — an average of 6.8 km/session, including at least one >10 km run. However, given persistent <7h sleep on all 14 recent nights and only adequate (not recovered) readiness, chasing this volume is inadvisable and risks reinforcing fatigue debt; maintain current sustainable rhythm instead.

insights.title: Chronic sleep debt correlates with elevated Running Economy (worse values)
insights.body: Despite improved HR and TE, Running Economy recently spiked to 253.5 ml/kg/km (‘Recreational’ rating) — the highest in the recent series — while sleep remains stuck at 4.8h avg and every single night in the past 14 has been <7h. Poor sleep impairs neuromuscular coordination and metabolic efficiency, directly explaining the economy dip.

insights.title: ACWR stability masks underlying recovery imbalance
insights.body: ACWR is optimal (0.8), but recovery balance jumped from 0.8 (4-wk avg) to 1.17 (latest) — driven entirely by HRV surge (+5.3 ms), not load reduction (acute load dropped only slightly to 173 from 249–638 in prior weeks). This suggests the body is rebounding *from* prior overload, not operating from a rested baseline.

insights.title: Cadence-HR dissociation reveals improved neuromuscular relaxation
insights.body: Cadence rose sharply (+32 spm) while avg HR fell (-7 bpm) and aerobic TE improved (-0.4), even as pace slowed (+23 sec/km). This triad confirms reduced neuromuscular tension and greater movement economy at sub-threshold intensities — a hallmark of effective aerobic base development.

insights.title: Aerobic decoupling is improving alongside VO2max gains
insights.body: Latest decoupling is 4.8% (just under the 5% aerobic threshold), down from median recent value of 7.11%; concurrently, VO2max rose +1.8 vs baseline (+4.8%) to 40.0. This confirms that recent training is strengthening aerobic endurance — not just capacity — and that fatigue resistance is increasing.
